desc:
In one move you may pick any element of nums and increase it by 1. Return the minimum number of moves needed to make all elements pairwise distinct. Values may grow beyond the original maximum.

For example, [3, 2, 1, 2, 1, 7] needs 6 moves: the sorted values 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 7 can become 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7.
hints: Only the multiset of values matters, not the positions. What does the smallest valid arrangement look like if the values were sorted?
Process values from small to large. A value that occurs several times must spread over consecutive free slots: one copy stays, the others move up.

Sweep v over the range with a carry of surplus copies. At each v, add cnt[v] to the pending copies, let one of them settle at v, and pay the number of copies still pending (each moves one step further). Continue past the max value until the carry is empty.
editorial: Count occurrences per value and sweep upward from 0. Keep pending, the number of elements that are waiting for a free slot at or above the current value. At value v, pending += cnt[v]. If pending > 0, one element settles at v (pending -= 1); every other pending element has to move to v + 1, which costs pending moves in total. Continue until the sweep is past the maximum and pending is zero.

The sweep covers at most max + n values, so the time is O(n + max). The greedy is optimal because moving an element past a free slot only increases the cost. Sorting and fixing each element to max(prev + 1, x) gives the same answer in O(n log n).
